en: Thus have I heard: Majjhima Nikāya 83, the Maghadeva Sutta.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Mithilā in the Maghadeva Mango Grove.
Then, in a certain place, the Blessed One broke into a smile.
Thereupon, it occurred to the Venerable Ānanda:
“What, indeed, is the cause, what is the reason for the Blessed One’s manifestation of a smile?
Tathāgatas do not manifest a smile without a reason.
Then the Venerable Ānanda, having arranged his robe over one shoulder and extending his joined palms in reverential salutation toward the Blessed One, said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason for the Blessed One’s manifestation of a smile?
Tathāgatas do not manifest a smile without a reason.
“Formerly, Ānanda, in this very Mithilā there was a king named Maghadeva—a righteous king of Dharma, established in Dharma, a great monarch.”
He practiced the Dhamma among brahmins and householders, both in the towns and in the countryside;
and he observed the Uposatha on the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the lunar fortnight.
Then, Ānanda, after the passing of many years, many hundreds of years, and many thousands of years, King Makhādeva addressed his barber:
“‘When you see, my dear barber, that grey hairs have grown upon my head, then you should inform me,’ he said.
‘Yes, Your Majesty,’ the barber replied to King Makhādeva.
Then, Ānanda, after the passing of many years, many hundreds of years, and many thousands of years, the barber saw that grey hairs had grown upon King Makhādeva’s head.”
Having seen him, he said this to King Makhādeva:
“The divine messengers have appeared for Your Majesty; grey hairs are seen growing upon your head.
“In that case, my dear barber, pull those grey hairs out carefully with the tweezers and place them in my joined palms.”
‘So be it, Your Majesty,’ Ānanda, the barber replied to King Makhādeva. Having carefully plucked out those grey hairs with a pair of tweezers, he placed them in the joined palms of King Makhādeva.
Then, Ānanda, King Makhādeva gave a choice village to the barber, summoned his eldest son, the prince, and said this to him:
‘My son, prince, the divine messengers have appeared to me.’”
Grey hairs are seen to have grown upon my head;
I have indeed enjoyed human pleasures;
it is now time to seek divine pleasures.
"Come, dear prince, take over this kingdom.
As for me, however, having shaved off my hair and beard and donned saffron robes, I shall go forth from the household life into homelessness.
Therefore, dear prince, when you too see grey hairs grown upon your head, then [inform] the barber..."

Having given away the best of your cattle and having thoroughly instructed your eldest son in the kingdom, you should shave off your hair and beard, don saffron robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness.
You should carry on this noble practice that I have established; do not be the last man of my lineage.
“Dear prince, when such a noble practice as this is interrupted during the lifetime of a generation of men, he who causes that interruption is the last man of that lineage.
Therefore, dear prince, I say this to you:
‘May you continue this noble practice established by me; do not become the last man of my line.’”
Then, Ānanda, King Makhādeva, having given a choice village to his barber and having thoroughly instructed his eldest son,
the prince, in the kingdom, shaved off his hair and beard right here in this Makhādeva mango grove,
donned saffron robes, and went forth from the household life into homelessness.
Thus, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, he dwelt pervading one quarter, likewise the second, likewise the third,
and likewise the fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwelt pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—
vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
With a mind imbued with compassion...
with a mind imbued with sympathetic joy...
with a mind imbued with equanimity, he dwelt pervading one direction, likewise the second, likewise the third.

Likewise the fourth. Thus, above, below, across, and everywhere, to all as himself, he dwelt pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
Furthermore, Ānanda, King Makhādeva spent eighty-four thousand years in princely play, and eighty-four thousand years...
He ruled as viceroy; he reigned for eighty-four thousand years;
and for eighty-four thousand years, having gone forth from the home life into homelessness right here in this very Makhādeva Mango Grove, he lived the holy life.
Having developed the four divine abodes, with the breakup of the body, after death, he was reborn in the Brahma world.
Then, Ānanda, after the passing of many years, many hundreds of years, and many thousands of years, King Makhādeva’s son addressed his barber:
“When you see, my dear barber, that grey hairs have grown upon my head, then inform me.
“Very well, Your Majesty,” the barber replied to King Makhādeva’s son.
After the passing of many years, many hundreds of years, and many thousands of years, Ānanda, the barber saw grey hairs growing on the head of King Makhādeva’s son.
Having seen them, he said this to King Makhādeva’s son:
“The divine messengers have appeared for Your Majesty.”
‘Grey hairs have grown upon my head.
‘In that case, friend barber, pull those grey hairs out carefully with the tweezers and place them in my joined palms.
‘Very well, Your Majesty,’ the barber replied to King Makhādeva’s son, and having pulled those grey hairs out carefully with the tweezers, he placed them in the king’s joined palms.
Then, Ānanda, King Makhādeva, having given the choice village to his barber and summoned his eldest son, the prince, said this to him:
“My son, prince, the messengers of the gods have appeared to me;
gray hairs are seen to have grown upon my head.”
"I have indeed enjoyed human pleasures;
it is now time to seek divine pleasures.
Come, dear prince, take charge of this kingdom."
"But I, having shaved off my hair and beard and donned saffron robes, shall go forth from the household life into homelessness.
Therefore, dear prince, when you too see grey hairs grown upon your head, then,
having given a choice village to your barber and having properly instructed your eldest son in the kingdom, shave off your hair and beard— "
“Having clothed yourself in saffron robes, you should go forth from the household life into homelessness.
You should carry on this noble practice that I have established; do not be the last man of my lineage.
For when a pair of men is present, dear prince, and such a noble practice comes to an end, he is the last man of that lineage.”
"Therefore, dear prince, I say this to you:
'May you carry on this noble practice that I have established; do not be the last man of my lineage.
Then, Ānanda, King Makhādeva, having given a choice village to his barber, [bestowed] his eldest son...
Having thoroughly instructed the prince in the kingdom, he shaved off his hair and beard right here in this Makhādeva Mango Grove,
donned saffron robes, and went forth from the home life into homelessness.
He dwelt pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, and likewise the second, and likewise the third.

Likewise the fourth. Thus, above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as himself, he dwelt pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
[He dwelt] with a mind imbued with compassion...
With a mind imbued with sympathetic joy...
with a mind imbued with equanimity, he dwelt pervading one quarter, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth;
thus above, below, across, everywhere, in all respects, the entire world, with a mind imbued with equanimity.
He dwelt having pervaded with a mind that was vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity,
and free from ill will. Now, Ānanda, King Makhādeva’s son played as a prince for eighty-four thousand years,
served as viceroy for eighty-four thousand years, and reigned as king for eighty-four thousand years.
For eighty-four thousand years, having gone forth from the home life into homelessness in this very Mango Grove of Makhādeva, he lived the holy life.
Having developed the four divine abodes, with the breakup of the body, after death, he was reborn in the Brahma-world.
Furthermore, Ānanda, the sons and grandsons of King Makhādeva, in succession, numbered eighty-four thousand kings.
In this very Mango Grove of Maghadeva, having shaved off their hair and beard and donned saffron robes,
they went forth from the home life into homelessness.
They dwelt having pervaded one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, and likewise the second, and likewise the third.

Likewise the fourth. Thus, above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as themselves, they dwelt pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
With a mind imbued with compassion...
With a mind accompanied by sympathetic joy...
with a mind accompanied by equanimity, they dwelt pervading one quarter, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth;
thus above, below, across, everywhere, in all respects, the entire world with a mind accompanied by equanimity.
They dwelt having pervaded with a mind that was vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
For eighty-four thousand years they played at the games of youth; for eighty-four thousand years they exercised the office of viceroy;
for eighty-four thousand years they ruled the kingdom; and for eighty-four thousand years right here...
In the Ambavana grove of Maghadeva, they went forth from the household life into homelessness and practiced the holy life.
Having developed the four divine abodes, at the breaking up of the body after death, they were reborn in the Brahma-world.
King Nimi was the last of them—a righteous king, a king of Dhamma, established in Dhamma, a great king.
He practices the Dhamma among brahmins and householders, among those in towns and those in the countryside;
and he observes the Uposatha on the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the lunar fortnight.
Once in the past, Ānanda, when the gods of the Thirty-three were seated together and assembled in the Sudhammā assembly hall, this discussion arose among them:
“It is indeed a gain for the people of Videha, it is truly a great fortune for the people of Videha,
that they have Nimi as their king— a righteous king, a king of Dhamma, a great monarch established in Dhamma;
he practices Dhamma among the brahmins and householders, and among the townspeople and the rural folk.”
‘And he observes the Uposatha on the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the fortnight.
Then, Ānanda, Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed the Tāvatiṃsa devas:
‘Would you like, sirs, to see King Nimi?’”
“‘We wish to see King Nimi, dear sir.
Now at that time, Ānanda, on the Uposatha day of the fifteenth, King Nimi had washed his head and, observing the Uposatha, was seated in the upper chamber of the palace.
Then, Ānanda, Sakka, lord of the devas—just as a strong man might bend or extend his arm—”
Just as one might stretch out an arm, or bend back an arm that has been stretched out, even so, having vanished among the Tāvatiṃsa gods,
he reappeared before King Nimi.
Then, Ānanda, Sakka, lord of the devas, said this to King Nimi:
“It is a gain for you, Great King; it is well-gained by you, Great King.
The gods of the Thirty-three, Great King, are seated in the Sudhamma assembly hall, praising you:
‘It is indeed a gain for the Videhans! It is truly well-gained by the Videhans!’”
"For those for whom King Nimi is a righteous king, a king of Dhamma, a great king established in Dhamma;
who practices Dhamma among brahmins and householders, in towns and in the countryside;
and who observes the Uposatha on the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the fortnight."
“The gods of the Thirty-three, Great King, desire to see you.
Therefore, Great King, I shall send for you a chariot of thoroughbred horses yoked in a team of a thousand;
mount this divine vehicle, Great King, without wavering.”
Ānanda, King Nimi consented by remaining silent.
Then, Ānanda, Sakka, lord of the devas, perceiving King Nimi’s consent—
just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm— so did he vanish from the presence of King Nimi and reappear among the Tavatiṃsa devas.
In this very way, having vanished from the presence of King Nimi, he reappeared among the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
Then, Ānanda, Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed his charioteer Mātali:
“Come, my dear Mātali, harness the chariot drawn by a team of a thousand thoroughbreds, approach King Nimi, and speak to him thus:”
“Great King, this chariot drawn by a thousand thoroughbreds has been sent for you by Sakka, Lord of the Devas.
Great King, mount this divine vehicle without hesitation.
“Very well, venerable sir,” Mātali the charioteer replied to Sakka, Lord of the Devas. Having harnessed the chariot drawn by a thousand thoroughbreds, he approached King Nimi and said this:
“Great King, this chariot yoked with a thousand thoroughbreds has been sent for you by Sakka, lord of the devas.
Ascend, Great King, upon this divine vehicle without wavering.

Moreover, Great King, by which path shall I lead you—to that by which those of evil deeds experience the result of their evil deeds, or to that by which those of wholesome deeds experience the result of their wholesome deeds?”
“‘Mātali, take me with both of you,’ he said.
Then, Ānanda, Mātali the charioteer brought King Nimi into the Sudhamma assembly hall.
Sakka, lord of the devas, saw King Nimi approaching from afar.”
Having seen King Nimi, he said this to him:
“Come, great king!
Welcome, great king!”
"O Great King, the gods of the Thirty-three, desiring to see you, have assembled in the Sudhamma hall, praising you thus:
'It is a gain for the people of Videha! It is a great fortune for the people of Videha that they have a king such as Nimi—a righteous king, a king of Dhamma, established in Dhamma, a great monarch!'"
"He practices the Dhamma among brahmins and householders, both in the towns and in the countryside;
and he observes the Uposatha on the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the fortnight.
"Those Tāvatiṃsa devas, Great King, desire to see him."
“Enjoy yourself, great king, among the gods by means of divine power.
“Enough, dear sir! Send me back right there to Mithilā.
There I shall practice the Dhamma among the brahmins and householders, both in the towns and in the countryside.”
"I observe the Uposatha on the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the fortnight.
Then, Ānanda, Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed his charioteer Mātali:
"Come, dear Mātali, harness the chariot drawn by a thousand thoroughbreds and take King Nimi right back to Mithilā."
“Yes, venerable sir,” Mātali the charioteer replied to Sakka, lord of the devas. Having yoked the royal chariot drawn by a thousand thoroughbreds, he brought King Nimi right back to Mithilā.

There, Ānanda, King Nimi practiced the Dhamma among the brahmins and householders, both in the towns and in the countryside; and he observed the Uposatha on the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the lunar fortnight.
Then, Ānanda, after the passing of many years, many hundreds of years, and many thousands of years, King Nimi addressed his barber:
“When you see, my dear barber, that grey hairs have grown upon my head, then report it to me.
“Very well, Your Majesty,” the barber replied to King Nimi.
After the passing of many years, many hundreds of years, and many thousands of years, Ānanda, the barber saw grey hairs growing on King Nimi’s head.
Having seen them, he said to King Nimi:
“The divine messengers have appeared for your majesty.”
‘Grey hairs have grown upon my head. [The king said:
‘In that case, my dear barber, pull out those grey hairs carefully with the tweezers and place them in my joined palms.
‘Yes, sire,’ the barber replied to King Nimi, and having pulled out those grey hairs carefully with the tweezers, he placed them in King Nimi’s joined palms.
Then, Ānanda, King Nimi, having given a choice village to his barber and summoned his eldest son, the prince, said this to him:
“My son, dear prince, the messengers of the gods have appeared to me;
gray hairs are seen to have grown upon my head.”
"I have indeed enjoyed human pleasures;
it is now time to seek divine pleasures.
Come, dear prince, take charge of this kingdom."
"But I shall shave off my hair and beard, don saffron robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness.
Therefore, dear prince, when you too see grey hairs grown upon your head, then,
having given a choice village to your barber and having properly instructed your eldest son in the kingdom, shave off your hair and beard..."
"Clad in saffron robes, you should go forth from the home life into homelessness.
You should continue this noble practice that has been established by me; do not be the last man of my lineage.
For in whatever generation of men such a noble practice comes to an end, dear prince, he is considered the last man of that lineage."
"Therefore, dear prince, I say this to you:
'May you carry on this noble practice that I have established; do not be the last man of my line.
Then, Ānanda, King Nimi, having given a choice village to his barber, [entrusted] his eldest son, the prince, with great care...
Having ruled the kingdom, right here in this Makhādeva Mango Grove, he shaved off his hair and beard, donned saffron robes, and went forth from the home life into homelessness.
He dwelt pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness; likewise the second, likewise the third.

Likewise the fourth. Thus, above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as himself, he dwelt pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
[He dwelt] with a mind imbued with compassion...
With a mind accompanied by sympathetic joy...
with a mind accompanied by equanimity, he dwelt pervading one quarter, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth;
thus above, below, across, everywhere, in all respects, the entire world, with a mind accompanied by equanimity.
Having pervaded with a mind that was vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will, he dwelt.

Furthermore, Ānanda, King Nimi played as a prince for eighty-four thousand years, served as viceroy for eighty-four thousand years, and ruled the kingdom for eighty-four thousand years. He [reigned] for eighty-four thousand years.
In this very Mango Grove of Maghadeva, he went forth from the household life into homelessness and lived the holy life.
Having developed the four divine abodes, with the breakup of the body, after death, he was reborn in the Brahma-world.
Now, Ānanda, King Nimi had a son named Kaḷārajanaka.
He did not go forth from the home life into homelessness;
he cut off that virtuous practice;
he became the very last man among them.
Now, Ānanda, it might occur to you:
"Perhaps at that time Rājā Makhādeva was someone else who established that auspicious practice.
But, Ānanda, this should not be viewed in such a way.
At that time, I was King Makhādeva.
I established that wholesome practice; having established that wholesome practice, later generations followed it.

But that good practice, Ānanda, does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, nor to Nibbāna; it leads only as far as rebirth in the Brahma-world.
However, this good practice now established by me, Ānanda, leads to utter disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna.
And what, Ānanda, is the wholesome practice now established by me that leads to utter disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna?
It is this very Noble Eightfold Path; namely:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
“Ānanda, this is the noble practice now established by me that leads to utter disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna.
Therefore, Ānanda, I say this to you:
‘You should continue this noble practice established by me; do not become the last men of my lineage.’”
“Ānanda, when a pair of men exists in whom such a noble practice as this is cut off, they are the last of their lineage.
Therefore, Ānanda, I say this to you:
‘You should continue this noble practice that I have established; do not become the last of my lineage.’”
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The Venerable Ānanda, being uplifted, rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The third discourse, the Maghadeva Sutta, is concluded.
